newsitem.title: UK: NWE FUEL OIL BARGES A LITTLE HIGHER, CARGOES STEADY.
newsitem.headline: NWE FUEL OIL BARGES A LITTLE HIGHER, CARGOES STEADY.

text.p: Euro high sulphur fuel barges edged higher late on Tuesday with some traders arguing it reflected scarce prompt supply while others saw a market being artificially held up by some players.

Traders said high sulphur barges traded at least twice at $96 fob in Rotterdam and Antwerp late in the day after earlier trades between $94.50 and $95.50 fob ARA, compared with Monday level of $93.50 to $95.
Traders said the higher numbers were done for very prompt material which remains in short supply, especially with two refiners offering little. Others disputed this.
"I bought 5,000 tonnes from a refiner at $94.25 and sold at $95...I think the market is held artificially high by a major," a trader with a major said.

One trader said that although the price difference between barges and cargoes was wide and seemed unusual, high sulphur cargoes were not moving into barges due to high freight and the fact that little was available.
"This is one of those times when there's a huge difference between the fob and cif quotes and it happens at a time of scarcity on the barge market," he said.
High sulphur cargoes were pegged around $93/$94 cif for utility spec but one bid came in from an end user at below $89, a number discounted by sellers as too low.
A second end user was also heard to be a prospective buyer as well as a major but two European power utilities were unlikely to be buyers now, traders said.

There was unconfirmed talk of a trader coming into the market with an 80,000-tonne cargo originally destined to go to the United States, but forced to stay in NWE due to a narrow arbitrage window. But some traders said a vessel that size would be difficult to place in NWE.
Russian cracked material was $1 softer, with one seller saying he would do two means+$1 for cracked M-100.
"The buyers are relaxed. They see the stuff is out there. For sure I will not get the premiums I was getting last week," the seller, an independent trader, said.
One percent was talked a little up with few cargoes seen on offer. One seller said that he had turned down bids of $96/$97 -- the offer level of front month swaps.
"I see the market moving up and I'm looking for a floating price," a trader with the seller said.

Shipping brokers said a U.S. major was enquiring about 75,000 tonnes of low sulphur fuel oil loading end month to go trans-Atlantic. But some traders said the major usually takes VGO or low sulphur straight-run to the U.S, not one percent.
Low sulphur barge offers moved a little higher to $97/$97.50, but buying interest was virtually nil, even for sellers $1 lower.
"We've blended our material in our high sulphur pool because we can't sell. If I see any buyer at $96/96.50 we'll take him out but there's no buying," a seller said.
